title: Chinese Remainder Theorem, Fermat, RSA
summary: Solving systems of congruences with the Chinese Remainder Theorem, shrinking huge powers with Fermat’s little theorem, the Fermat primality test and its pseudoprimes, and RSA. Expect a CRT system, a big-power computation and an RSA encrypt/decrypt, plus the proof of why RSA decryption works.

blocks.text: If you know a number's remainders for several coprime moduli, you know the number itself, up to their product.

blocks.name: Chinese Remainder Theorem
blocks.text: Let m₁, …, mₙ be pairwise relatively prime positive integers greater than 1, and a₁, …, aₙ any integers. Then the system x ≡ a₁ (mod m₁), …, x ≡ aₙ (mod mₙ) has a unique solution modulo M = m₁m₂⋯mₙ: there is a solution with 0 ≤ x < M, and every other solution is congruent to it mod M.

proof.text: Existence: the construction below produces a solution.

Uniqueness: if x and y both solve the system, then mᵢ | x − y for every i. The mᵢ are pairwise coprime, so their product M divides x − y (apply “gcd(a, b) = 1, a | c, b | c ⇒ ab | c” repeatedly). So x ≡ y (mod M). ∎

blocks.text: Think of a combination lock with several dials, of sizes 3, 7 and 10, that all click forward together. After x clicks, the dials read x mod 3, x mod 7, x mod 10. CRT says that when the dial sizes share no common factor, the readings determine x exactly, up to a full cycle of 3·7·10 = 210 clicks.

blocks.title: CRT construction (formula)
items: M = m₁⋯mₙ, and for each i, Mᵢ = M / mᵢ (the product of all the other moduli).
Find yᵢ = an inverse of Mᵢ mod mᵢ: Mᵢyᵢ ≡ 1 (mod mᵢ). It exists because gcd(Mᵢ, mᵢ) = 1.
x = a₁M₁y₁ + a₂M₂y₂ + ⋯ + aₙMₙyₙ, then reduce mod M.

blocks.text: Why it works: mod mᵢ, every term except the i-th has a factor of mᵢ inside Mⱼ (j ≠ i), so it's ≡ 0. The i-th term is aᵢ·(Mᵢyᵢ) ≡ aᵢ·1. So x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ) for every i. Each term is a “switch” that is 1 on its own dial and 0 on all the others.
A smaller one: x ≡ 1 (mod 2), x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 4 (mod 5) has M = 30, and the solution is x ≡ 29 (mod 30).
The moduli must be pairwise relatively prime. x ≡ 0 (mod 2) and x ≡ 1 (mod 4) has no solution: the first makes x even, the second makes x odd.
Lock it down

blocks.title: The CRT construction
items: Check that the moduli are pairwise coprime: test every pair, not just all of them together.
Draw a table with one row per congruence and columns mᵢ, aᵢ, Mᵢ, Mᵢ mod mᵢ, yᵢ, aᵢMᵢyᵢ.
Compute M = m₁m₂⋯mₙ. For each row, Mᵢ = product of the other moduli (cover up your own and multiply the rest).
Shrink Mᵢ mod mᵢ to a small number. Find its inverse mod mᵢ by trying 1, 2, 3, …. That inverse is yᵢ.
Fill in the last column and add it up: x = Σ aᵢMᵢyᵢ. Reduce mod M.
Check: divide your x by each mᵢ and confirm the remainder is aᵢ. Write the answer as x ≡ … (mod M).

blocks.title: Back-substitution
items: If a congruence has a coefficient, like cx ≡ a (mod m), first multiply by c̄ to get it into the form x ≡ … (mod m).
Start with the congruence that has the biggest modulus (fewer steps later). Turn it into an equation: x = a₁ + m₁t.
Plug that into the next congruence: a₁ + m₁t ≡ a₂ (mod m₂). Reduce the numbers mod m₂ and solve for t, using the recipe. You get t ≡ t₀ (mod m₂).
Write t = t₀ + m₂u and substitute back: x = (a₁ + m₁t₀) + m₁m₂u. You now know x mod m₁m₂.
Treat this as your new “first” congruence and repeat with the next one, until all are used.
Check: test the final x in every original congruence (including any with a coefficient).

blocks.title: construction with nontrivial inverses
steps: M₁ = 35 ≡ 3 (mod 4); 3·3 = 9 ≡ 1, so y₁ = 3 — inverse of M₁ mod 4
M₂ = 28 ≡ 3 (mod 5); 3·2 = 6 ≡ 1, so y₂ = 2 — inverse of M₂ mod 5
M₃ = 20 ≡ 6 (mod 7); 6·6 = 36 ≡ 1, so y₃ = 6 — inverse of M₃ mod 7

blocks.title: back-substitution with a coefficient
steps: x ≡ 3·3 = 9 ≡ 4 (mod 5) — inverse of 2 mod 5 is 3; multiply both sides by it
x = 5 + 8(3 + 5u) = 29 + 40u — substitute t = 3 + 5u; now x is known mod 40

blocks.text: Wrong: taking yᵢ = Mᵢ mod mᵢ, e.g. y₂ = 2 in the first example (where M₂ = 30 ≡ 2 mod 7). Right: yᵢ is the inverse of that number, so y₂ = 4. (yᵢ is the thing that turns Mᵢ into 1 mod mᵢ.)
Wrong: finding the inverse of Mᵢ mod M, or the inverse of mᵢ mod Mᵢ. Right: the inverse of Mᵢ mod the small modulus mᵢ. (The “switch” only has to read 1 on its own dial.)
Wrong: giving 779 as the final answer. Right: reduce mod M: x ≡ 79 (mod 140). (The answer is a whole class mod M, so always give the modulus too.)
Wrong: “6, 10, 15 have gcd 1, so CRT applies.” Right: CRT needs every pair coprime, and gcd(6, 10) = 2. (Shared factors can make the congruences contradict each other.)
Wrong: in back-substitution, solving 5 + 8t ≡ 4 mod 8. Right: solve it mod 5, the modulus of the congruence you are plugging into. (Mod 8 the 8t just disappears and you learn nothing.)
Non-coprime moduli: x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) is solvable iff a ≡ b (mod gcd(m, n)), and then the solution is unique mod lcm(m, n). Example: x ≡ 5 (mod 12), x ≡ 11 (mod 18) gives x ≡ 29 (mod 36).

lesson.title: Fermat’s little theorem: shrinking powers and inverses

blocks.text: Mod a prime p, a<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1 (when p ∤ a). So exponents can be shrunk mod p − 1.
(x + y)ⁿ = Σₖ C(n, k) xⁿ⁻ᵏyᵏ where C(n, k) = n! / (k!(n − k)!), the rows of Pascal's triangle.
E.g. (x + y)⁷ = x⁷ + 7x⁶y + 21x⁵y² + 35x⁴y³ + 35x³y⁴ + 21x²y⁵ + 7xy⁶ + y⁷. Notice 7 divides every middle coefficient.

blocks.name: Freshman’s dream
blocks.text: If p is prime and 1 ≤ k ≤ p − 1, then p | C(p, k). Hence (x + y)ᵖ ≡ xᵖ + yᵖ (mod p).

proof.text: C(p, k) = p! / (k!(p − k)!). The prime p appears in the numerator p! but not in k! or (p − k)!, since all their factors are less than p. So p survives in C(p, k). In the binomial expansion of (x + y)ᵖ only the two end terms are not multiples of p.

blocks.name: Fermat's little theorem (Rosen Thm 3)
blocks.text: If p is prime and a is an integer not divisible by p, then aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p). Furthermore, for every integer a, aᵖ ≡ a (mod p).

proof.text: (For a ≥ 1; negative a follow by reducing mod p.) Write a = 1 + 1 + ⋯ + 1 (a ones) and apply the Freshman's dream over and over: aᵖ = (1 + (a − 1))ᵖ ≡ 1ᵖ + (a − 1)ᵖ ≡ 1ᵖ + 1ᵖ + (a − 2)ᵖ ≡ ⋯ ≡ 1ᵖ + ⋯ + 1ᵖ = a (mod p). So aᵖ ≡ a. If p ∤ a, then gcd(a, p) = 1, so we can cancel one a (cancellation law): aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p).

blocks.text: Mod a prime p (and p ∤ a), exponents only matter mod p − 1. Write the exponent as q(p − 1) + r; then aⁿ = (aᵖ⁻¹)^q · aʳ ≡ 1^q · aʳ = aʳ.
Reduce the exponent mod p − 1, not mod p. And it needs p prime and p ∤ a.

blocks.name: Inverses via Fermat
blocks.text: If p is prime and p ∤ a, then a⁻¹ ≡ aᵖ⁻² (mod p).

proof.text: a · aᵖ⁻² = aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p) by Fermat.

blocks.title: Inverse and a congruence via Fermat
blocks.prompt: Use Fermat to find 4⁻¹ mod 13, then solve 4x ≡ 5 (mod 13).

blocks.title: Shrink a big power aⁿ mod a prime p
items: Make sure p is prime. If it isn't, Fermat does not apply: use repeated squaring, or split the modulus into primes and use CRT.
Reduce the base: replace a by a mod p. If that is 0, the answer is 0. Stop.
Divide the exponent by p − 1: n = q(p − 1) + r. Throw away q and keep only r. The q copies of aᵖ⁻¹ each equal 1, like full laps around a track that put you back at the start.
If r = 0, the answer is 1. Otherwise compute aʳ mod p, reducing after every multiplication.
Shortcut: look for a small power that is ±1, like 3³ = 27 ≡ −1 (mod 7). Then big powers become powers of −1.
Check: multiply back, q(p − 1) + r must equal the original exponent n, and your answer must be in 0 to p − 1.

blocks.title: exponent shrink plus the −1 trick
steps: 5² = 25 ≡ 12 ≡ −1 (mod 13) — look for a small power that is ±1

blocks.text: Wrong: reducing the exponent mod p: for 3¹⁰⁰ mod 7, using 100 mod 7 = 2 to get 3² ≡ 2. Right: 100 mod 6 = 4, so 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 4. (The cycle length is p − 1, because that is the exponent Fermat makes equal to 1.)
Wrong: 21⁵⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 7) “by Fermat.” Right: 21 ≡ 0 (mod 7), so 21⁵⁰ ≡ 0. (Fermat needs p ∤ a. Always reduce the base first.)

Wrong: for 6⁴⁰ mod 11, “40 leaves remainder 0 mod 10, so the answer is 0.” Right: 40 = 4·10 + 0, so the answer is 6⁰ = 1. (Remainder 0 in the exponent means “exactly some full laps,” which lands on 1.)
Wrong: treating 15 like a prime: 2¹⁰⁰ mod 15 with 100 mod 14 = 2, giving 4. Right: the real answer is 1 (2⁴ = 16 ≡ 1 mod 15). (Fermat's shortcut only works for a prime modulus.)

lesson.title: Fermat test, pseudoprimes and Carmichael numbers

blocks.name: Fermat test
blocks.text: Given n, pick a with 0 < a < n. If aⁿ⁻¹ ≢ 1 (mod n), then n is definitely not prime (contrapositive of Fermat). If aⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1, n may or may not be prime.
Example: 2¹⁴ mod 15 = 4 ≠ 1 (since 2⁴ ≡ 1, 2¹⁴ ≡ 2² = 4), so 15 is composite, without finding a factor.
Modern primality tests (e.g. Miller–Rabin, used to find huge primes for cryptography) are built on this: pass many such tests and the probability n is prime is provably very high.

A composite n with bⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n) is a pseudoprime to the base b. A composite n that is a pseudoprime to every base b with gcd(b, n) = 1 is a Carmichael number; the smallest is 561 = 3·11·17. So the Fermat test alone can be fooled.

blocks.name: Undoing powers mod p
blocks.text: If p is prime and gcd(e, p − 1) = 1, then f(m) = mᵉ mod p is a one-to-one function on {0, …, p − 1}. Its inverse is g(c) = cᵈ mod p, where de − k(p − 1) = 1 (Bézout).

proof.text: g(f(m)) ≡ mᵈᵉ = m^{1 + k(p−1)} = m·(mᵖ⁻¹)ᵏ ≡ m·1ᵏ = m (mod p) by Fermat, for p ∤ m; and if m = 0 both sides are 0. So g undoes f, which forces f to be injective.

blocks.text: Example: p = 7, e = 5 (gcd(5, 6) = 1). 5·5 = 25 = 4·6 + 1, so d = 5. Then f(3) = 3⁵ mod 7 = 5 and g(5) = 5⁵ mod 7 = 3. ✓ Modular powers otherwise behave “randomly” enough to be used in pseudorandom number generators.
With e = 2 (gcd(2, 6) = 2) it fails: 1² ≡ 6² ≡ 1 (mod 7). The fifth powers of 0, …, 6 mod 7 are 0, 1, 4, 5, 2, 3, 6, all different. This is RSA with a single prime.

blocks.title: The Fermat test (prove n is composite)
items: Pick a base a with 1 < a < n; 2 is the usual choice. If gcd(a, n) > 1 you have already found a factor, so n is composite.
Compute aⁿ⁻¹ mod n by repeated squaring: list a, a², a⁴, a⁸, … mod n, write n − 1 as a sum of powers of 2, and multiply the matching entries.
Do not shrink the exponent mod n − 1. That trick assumes n is prime, which is exactly what you are testing.
If the result is not 1: n is composite. Say why: “if n were prime, Fermat's little theorem would give 1.”
If the result is 1: the test is inconclusive. n is prime or a pseudoprime to base a. You may try another base (Carmichael numbers pass every coprime base).
Check: recheck the squares table; each entry must be the one above it squared, mod n.

blocks.title: Fermat test on n = 21, base 2
blocks.prompt: Use the Fermat test with base 2 to decide whether 21 is prime.
steps: 20 = 16 + 4 — n − 1 as a sum of powers of 2
blocks.answer: 2²⁰ ≡ 4 ≢ 1 (mod 21), so 21 is composite. If 21 were prime, Fermat would force the answer 1. We never had to find the factors 3 and 7.

blocks.text: Wrong: “2⁵⁶⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 561), so 561 is prime.” Right: 561 = 3·11·17. (Passing the test proves nothing. Only failing it proves something: that n is composite.)

blocks.title: A pseudoprime caught by another base
blocks.prompt: Show 341 = 11·31 passes the Fermat test to base 2 but fails it to base 3.
steps: 2³⁴⁰ = (2¹⁰)³⁴ ≡ 1 (mod 341): 341 passes base 2, so it is a pseudoprime to the base 2.
So base 3 proves 341 is composite. Carmichael numbers like 561 pass every coprime base, so no number of Fermat tests can certify primality.
blocks.answer: 341 is a base-2 pseudoprime; 3³⁴⁰ ≡ 56 (mod 341) shows it is composite

blocks.text: Anyone can encrypt with the public key (n, e). Only someone who knows how n factors can compute d and decrypt.

Alice hands out open padlocks to everyone (the public encryption function f) but keeps the only key (the secret decryption function g, with g(f(m)) = m). Anyone can snap a message shut, but only Alice can open it. Knowing how to compute f and seeing f(m) should not let an eavesdropper (Eve) recover m. Scary fact: nobody has proved this is actually hard. It's a very important open problem.

blocks.title: The RSA system
items: Alice privately picks two large primes p, q and sets n = pq.
She chooses e with gcd(e, (p − 1)(q − 1)) = 1.
Public key: (n, e). Encryption: c = f(m) = mᵉ mod n.
Private key: using extended Euclid she finds d with de ≡ 1 (mod (p − 1)(q − 1)). Decryption: m = g(c) = cᵈ mod n.
She keeps p, q, d and (p − 1)(q − 1) secret.

blocks.text: Encrypting and decrypting both use fast modular exponentiation.

blocks.name: RSA decryption works
blocks.text: With n = pq (p ≠ q primes), de ≡ 1 (mod (p − 1)(q − 1)): g(f(m)) = m for all 0 ≤ m < n.

proof.text: Write de = 1 + k(p − 1)(q − 1) with k ≥ 0. Then g(f(m)) ≡ (mᵉ)ᵈ = m · m^{k(p−1)(q−1)} (mod n).
Mod p (Fermat): if p ∤ m, Fermat gives mᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1, so m^{k(p−1)(q−1)} = (mᵖ⁻¹)^{k(q−1)} ≡ 1 and mᵈᵉ ≡ m (mod p). If p | m, both sides are 0 mod p.
Mod q: the same argument with p and q swapped gives mᵈᵉ ≡ m (mod q).
Combine (CRT uniqueness): mᵈᵉ and m solve the same system mod p and mod q, with p, q coprime, so mᵈᵉ ≡ m (mod pq = n).
Both g(f(m)) and m lie in {0, …, n − 1}, so they are equal. ∎

blocks.title: Tiny RSA: keys, encrypt, decrypt
blocks.prompt: p = 3, q = 11, e = 3. Find the keys, encrypt m = 4 and decrypt the result.
steps: n = 33, (p − 1)(q − 1) = 2·10 = 20; gcd(3, 20) = 1, so e = 3 is allowed. Public key (33, 3).
blocks.answer: Public (33, 3), d = 7, c = 31, decrypts back to 4

blocks.text: Security: anyone who could factor n into p·q could compute (p − 1)(q − 1), then d, and decrypt. RSA’s security rests on factoring huge n being infeasible, so real keys use primes with hundreds of digits. A large quantum computer running Shor’s algorithm would break RSA.
Lock it down
Below, φ is short for (p − 1)(q − 1).

blocks.title: Set up an RSA key
items: Pick two different primes p and q. Compute n = pq.
Compute φ = (p − 1)(q − 1). This number is secret.
Pick e with 1 < e < φ and gcd(e, φ) = 1. Quick screen: φ is always even, so e must be odd; also rule out any e sharing a prime factor with φ.
Run extended Euclid on φ and e to get 1 = d·e + t·φ. d is the coefficient on e. Reduce it so 0 < d < φ (if negative, add φ).
Check: d·e mod φ = 1.
Publish (n, e). Keep p, q, φ and d secret.

blocks.title: Encrypt or decrypt (repeated squaring)
items: Encrypt: c = mᵉ mod n (the message must satisfy 0 ≤ m < n). Decrypt: m = cᵈ mod n. Same machine, different exponent.
Write the exponent as a sum of powers of 2, e.g. 23 = 16 + 4 + 2 + 1.
Make a squares table: x, x², x⁴, x⁸, …, each line the one above squared, reduced mod n. Negative stand-ins are fine and save work (49 ≡ −2 mod 51).
Multiply the table entries you need, reducing mod n after each multiplication so numbers stay small.
Check: after decrypting, re-encrypt your m with e. You must get c back.

blocks.title: Explain why decryption works (proof outline)
items: Since de ≡ 1 (mod φ), write de = 1 + k(p − 1)(q − 1) for some integer k.
Then cᵈ ≡ (mᵉ)ᵈ = m · m^{k(p−1)(q−1)} (mod n).
Mod p: if p ∤ m, Fermat gives mᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1, so m^{k(p−1)(q−1)} = (mᵖ⁻¹)^{k(q−1)} ≡ 1, and mᵉᵈ ≡ m (mod p). If p | m, both sides are 0 mod p.
Mod q: the same argument with the roles of p and q swapped.
So mᵉᵈ and m both solve x ≡ m (mod p), x ≡ m (mod q). p and q are distinct primes, so CRT uniqueness gives mᵉᵈ ≡ m (mod n).
Both cᵈ mod n and m lie in 0 to n − 1, so they are equal.
Check yourself: can you say where Fermat is used (steps 3 and 4) and where CRT is used (step 5)? Those are the two ideas graders look for.

blocks.title: build a key with Euclid, then encrypt
blocks.prompt: p = 5, q = 11, e = 7. Find the public and private keys, then encrypt m = 2.
steps: gcd(7, 40) = 1 — 7 is prime and does not divide 40, so e is valid
c = 2⁷ = 128 = 2·55 + 18, so c = 18 — encrypt: mᵉ mod n
blocks.answer: public key (55, 7), private d = 23, ciphertext c = 18. Check: 7·23 = 161 = 4·40 + 1 ✓.

blocks.title: play Eve: factor n, find d, decrypt
blocks.prompt: Eve sees the public key (n, e) = (51, 5) and the ciphertext c = 7. Since n is tiny, she can factor it. Recover m.
steps: 5·13 = 65 = 2·32 + 1, so d = 13 — inverse of e mod φ
13 = 8 + 4 + 1 — d as a sum of powers of 2
blocks.answer: m = 40. Check by re-encrypting: 40 ≡ −11, (−11)² = 121 ≡ 19, 19² = 361 ≡ 4, so 40⁵ ≡ 4·40 = 160 ≡ 7 = c ✓. This is exactly why real RSA uses primes hundreds of digits long.

blocks.text: Wrong: d = inverse of e mod n. Right: d = inverse of e mod φ = (p − 1)(q − 1). (Exponents cycle with Fermat's p − 1 and q − 1, not with n.)
Wrong: φ = n − 1, e.g. 54 for n = 55. Right: φ = (5 − 1)(11 − 1) = 40. (n − 1 would be right only if n were prime.)
Wrong: choosing e = 3 when p = 7, q = 13. Right: φ = 72 = 2³·3², so e = 3 shares a factor with φ and no d exists. Pick something like e = 5. (gcd(e, φ) = 1 is what makes d exist.)
Wrong: decrypting with e (computing cᵉ), or reducing mod φ instead of mod n. Right: m = cᵈ mod n. (φ is only for the exponent arithmetic; the message lives mod n.)
Wrong: keeping d = −17 from Bézout. Right: add φ to get d = 23. (Repeated squaring needs a positive exponent.)

cards.front: Solve x ≡ 2 (mod 3), x ≡ 3 (mod 4).
Why doesn't the CRT apply to x ≡ 1 (mod 4), x ≡ 2 (mod 6)?

back.text: 4 and 6 aren't coprime. In fact there's no solution: the first makes x odd, the second makes it even.

cards.front: Compute 2¹⁰⁰ mod 7.
Why can't you use Fermat to compute 3¹⁰⁰ mod 9?

back.text: 9 isn't prime (and 3 divides 9 anyway).

cards.front: 2¹⁴ mod 15 = 4. What does that prove?

back.text: 15 is composite. A prime p would give 2^(p−1) ≡ 1.

cards.front: p = 3, q = 11, e = 7. Find n, (p − 1)(q − 1), and d.
Encrypt m = 2 with the public key (33, 7).
What would Eve need in order to find d?

back.text: (p − 1)(q − 1), which means factoring n.

cards.front: State the Chinese Remainder Theorem.

back.text: If m₁, …, mₙ are pairwise relatively prime, the system x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ) has a unique solution mod M = m₁⋯mₙ.

cards.front: CRT construction formula?

back.text: x = Σ aᵢMᵢyᵢ mod M, Mᵢ = M/mᵢ, yᵢ = Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ
Each term is ≡ aᵢ mod mᵢ and ≡ 0 mod every other modulus.

cards.front: Why does CRT need pairwise coprime moduli?

back.text: Uniqueness uses “each mᵢ | x − y ⇒ M | x − y”, which needs coprimality; existence needs Mᵢ invertible mod mᵢ. With shared factors the congruences can contradict: x ≡ 0 (mod 2), x ≡ 1 (mod 4).

cards.front: CRT with non-coprime moduli m, n?

back.text: Solvable iff a ≡ b (mod gcd(m, n)); then unique mod lcm(m, n).

cards.front: Fermat’s little theorem?

back.text: p prime, p ∤ a ⇒ aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p); always aᵖ ≡ a (mod p)

cards.front: How do you reduce aⁿ mod a prime p?

back.text: Reduce a mod p; reduce n mod p − 1 (not mod p); compute a^r. Remainder 0 gives 1 (if p ∤ a).

cards.front: Inverse of a mod a prime p via Fermat?

back.text: a⁻¹ ≡ aᵖ⁻² (mod p)

cards.front: What does the Fermat test prove?

back.text: If aⁿ⁻¹ ≢ 1 (mod n) then n is composite. If aⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 the test is inconclusive.

cards.front: Pseudoprime to base b? Carmichael number?

back.text: Composite n with bⁿ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod n). A Carmichael number is a pseudoprime to every coprime base; smallest is 561 = 3·11·17. Smallest base-2 pseudoprime: 341 = 11·31.

cards.front: RSA key setup?

items: n = pq
gcd(e, φ) = 1
d = e⁻¹ mod φ
public (n, e), private d

back.text: d is the inverse of e mod φ, not mod n.

cards.front: Why does RSA decryption recover m? Where are Fermat and CRT used?

back.text: de = 1 + k(p − 1)(q − 1). Mod p, Fermat (or p | m) gives m^{de} ≡ m; same mod q. CRT uniqueness (p, q coprime) gives m^{de} ≡ m (mod n).

cards.front: Why is RSA secure (as far as we know)?

back.text: Computing d needs (p − 1)(q − 1), which is as hard as factoring n; knowing φ and n gives p + q = n − φ + 1 and so p, q.

cards.front: Freshman’s dream?

back.text: (a + b)ᵖ ≡ aᵖ + bᵖ (mod p) for p prime
Every middle binomial coefficient C(p, k) is divisible by p.

prompt.text: Solve x ≡ 2 (mod 5), x ≡ 3 (mod 7), x ≡ 10 (mod 11) using the CRT construction (not trial and error).

solution.text: m = 385. Let M<sub>1</sub> = 77, M<sub>2</sub> = 55, M<sub>3</sub> = 35. Inverses: 77 ≡ 2 (mod 5), and its inverse is 3. 55 ≡ 6 (mod 7), inverse 6. 35 ≡ 2 (mod 11), inverse 6.
Tests: the CRT formula Σ akMkyk. Common mistake: using the inverse of Mk modulo m instead of modulo mk.

hard.title: CRT with non-coprime moduli

items: (a) Solve x ≡ 5 (mod 12), x ≡ 11 (mod 18).
(b) Show that x ≡ 3 (mod 12), x ≡ 8 (mod 18) has no solution.
(c) State the general rule.

hard.answer: (a) x ≡ 29 (mod 36) (b) contradiction mod 6 (3 vs 2) (c) solvable iff a ≡ b (mod gcd(m, n)); then unique mod lcm(m, n)

solution.text: (a) Substitute x = 5 + 12k: 12k ≡ 6 (mod 18). Divide by 6: 2k ≡ 1 (mod 3), so k ≡ 2 (mod 3). That gives x = 5 + 12(2 + 3j) = 29 + 36j, i.e. x ≡ 29 (mod 36).
(b) The first congruence gives x ≡ 3 (mod 6), since 6 | 12. The second gives x ≡ 2 (mod 6), since 6 | 18. These contradict each other.
(c) x ≡ a (mod m), x ≡ b (mod n) is solvable iff a ≡ b (mod gcd(m, n)), and then the solution is unique mod lcm(m, n).
Tests: CRT when the moduli aren’t coprime. Common mistake: answering mod 12·18 = 216 instead of lcm = 36.

prompt.text: How many x in [0, 1000] satisfy x² ≡ 1 (mod 1001)? Find them all. (1001 = 7·11·13.)

solution.text: By CRT, x² ≡ 1 (mod 1001) ⇔ x² ≡ 1 mod 7, mod 11 and mod 13. Modulo a prime p, p | (x − 1)(x + 1) forces x ≡ ±1. That is 2 choices for each prime, 2³ = 8 combinations, and CRT turns each combination into exactly one residue mod 1001.
They come in pairs x ↔ 1001 − x, i.e. flipping all three signs.
Tests: CRT as a bijection between residues mod 1001 and triples of residues. Common mistake: answering 2 (only ±1). Modulo a composite number, a polynomial can have more roots than its degree.

hard.title: Towers and huge exponents with Fermat

items: (a) Compute 3<sup>10<sup>100</sup></sup> mod 13.
(b) 2027 is prime. Compute 2<sup>2026</sup> mod 2027 and 2<sup>2028</sup> mod 2027.

solution.text: (a) Fermat: 312 ≡ 1 (mod 13), so reduce the exponent mod 12. Since 10² = 100 ≡ 4 (mod 12) and 4·10 = 40 ≡ 4, every 10k with k ≥ 2 is ≡ 4 (mod 12). So 310100 ≡ 3⁴ = 81 ≡ 3.
(b) Fermat gives 22026 ≡ 1 directly. Then 22028 ≡ 2² = 4.
Tests: reducing exponents mod p − 1, never mod p. Common mistake: in (a), concluding “10100 ≡ 0 (mod 12) because it’s a power of 10”. 12 = 4·3 and 3 ∤ 10.

hard.title: 2730 divides n¹³ − n

prompt.text: Prove that 2730 | n<sup>13</sup> − n for every integer n. (2730 = 2·3·5·7·13.) Why can’t 11 be added to this list?

hard.answer: Proved: for p ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7, 13}, p − 1 | 12 so n¹³ ≡ n (mod p); 11 fails since 10 ∤ 12 (2¹³ − 2 = 8190 is not a multiple of 11).

solution.text: Fix p ∈ {2, 3, 5, 7, 13}. Note that p − 1 ∈ {1, 2, 4, 6, 12} always divides 12.

items: If p | n, then both n<sup>13</sup> and n are ≡ 0.
Otherwise Fermat gives n<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1, so n<sup>12</sup> = (n<sup>p−1</sup>)<sup>12/(p−1)</sup> ≡ 1 and n<sup>13</sup> ≡ n.

solution.text: So each of these five distinct primes divides n<sup>13</sup> − n, and so does their product 2730. ∎
For 11, p − 1 = 10 doesn’t divide 12. Concretely, 2<sup>13</sup> − 2 = 8190 = 2·3²·5·7·13, which is not a multiple of 11.
Tests: spotting “p − 1 | exponent − 1”. Common mistake: forgetting the case p | n, where Fermat’s hypothesis fails.

hard.title: 561 is a Carmichael number

prompt.text: Prove that a<sup>560</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 561) for every a with gcd(a, 561) = 1, even though 561 = 3·11·17 is composite. What does this say about using Fermat’s theorem as a primality test?

hard.answer: Proved: a² ≡ 1 (mod 3), a¹⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 11), a¹⁶ ≡ 1 (mod 17) and 2, 10, 16 | 560; CRT gives a⁵⁶⁰ ≡ 1 (mod 561). The Fermat test can be fooled.

solution.text: gcd(a, 561) = 1 means a is coprime to 3, to 11 and to 17. Fermat gives a² ≡ 1 (mod 3), a<sup>10</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 11), a<sup>16</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 17). Since 560 = 2·280 = 10·56 = 16·35, raising to those powers gives a<sup>560</sup> ≡ 1 modulo each of 3, 11, 17. Because they are pairwise coprime, a<sup>560</sup> ≡ 1 (mod 561). ∎
So the converse of Fermat is false: a composite number can pass the test an−1 ≡ 1 for every coprime base. Such numbers are called Carmichael numbers.
Tests: applying Fermat prime by prime, then combining with CRT. Common mistake: applying Fermat with modulus 561 itself, which is not prime.

prompt.text: RSA with p = 17, q = 23, e = 3. (a) Find n, (p − 1)(q − 1) and d. (b) Encrypt M = 42. (c) Decrypt your ciphertext using CRT (mod 17 and mod 23 separately).

solution.text: Tests: every RSA step, plus CRT as a shortcut. Common mistake: computing d as an inverse mod n instead of mod (p − 1)(q − 1).

prompt.text: An RSA modulus is n = 4189 = pq. Someone leaks (p − 1)(q − 1) = 4060. Recover p and q. With e = 3, find d.

solution.text: Tests: understanding that knowing (p − 1)(q − 1) is as good as knowing the factorization. Common mistake: trying to factor 4189 by trial division (which works here, but not on an exam with large numbers) instead of using the sum-and-product trick.

hard.title: RSA works for every message

prompt.text: Prove that RSA decryption works for every message 0 ≤ M < n = pq, including M that share a factor with n: if ed ≡ 1 (mod (p − 1)(q − 1)), then Med ≡ M (mod n).

hard.answer: Proved: M^{ed} ≡ M mod p and mod q in both cases p | M and p ∤ M (Fermat), so pq | M^{ed} − M.

solution.text: Write ed = 1 + k(p − 1)(q − 1) with k ≥ 0.
Mod p. If p | M, both Med and M are ≡ 0. Otherwise Fermat gives Mp−1 ≡ 1, so Med = M · (Mp−1)k(q−1) ≡ M. In both cases p | Med − M.
Mod q. The same argument gives q | Med − M.
p and q are distinct primes, so pq | M<sup>ed</sup> − M. Since 0 ≤ M < n, decryption returns exactly M. ∎

Tests: splitting into prime moduli to get around the coprimality hypothesis. Common mistake: using a Fermat/Euler-type result modulo n directly. That needs gcd(M, n) = 1, which the problem explicitly doesn’t assume.

keyFacts: CRT: pairwise coprime mᵢ ⇒ unique x mod M = ∏ mᵢ; x = Σ aᵢMᵢyᵢ with yᵢ = Mᵢ⁻¹ mod mᵢ
Non-coprime: solvable iff a ≡ b (mod gcd(m, n)), unique mod lcm(m, n)
Fermat: p prime, p ∤ a ⇒ aᵖ⁻¹ ≡ 1 (mod p); reduce exponents mod p − 1
aⁿ⁻¹ ≢ 1 (mod n) proves n composite; ≡ 1 proves nothing (pseudoprimes, Carmichael 561)
RSA: n = pq, φ = (p − 1)(q − 1), gcd(e, φ) = 1, d = e⁻¹ mod φ; c = mᵉ mod n, m = cᵈ mod n
RSA works: Fermat mod p and mod q, then CRT uniqueness mod pq
Freshman’s dream: (a + b)ᵖ ≡ aᵖ + bᵖ (mod p)

parsons.title: Why RSA decryption recovers the message
parsons.goal: Let n = pq with distinct primes p, q, let de ≡ 1 (mod (p − 1)(q − 1)), and let 0 ≤ M < n with p ∤ M and q ∤ M. If C = Mᵉ mod n, prove Cᵈ mod n = M.
lines: Since C ≡ Mᵉ (mod n), Cᵈ ≡ M<sup>de</sup> (mod n); write de = 1 + t(p − 1)(q − 1) with an integer t ≥ 0.
Since p ∤ M, Fermat’s little theorem gives M<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod p), so M<sup>de</sup> = M·(M<sup>p−1</sup>)<sup>t(q−1)</sup> ≡ M (mod p).
The same argument with q (using M<sup>q−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod q)) gives M<sup>de</sup> ≡ M (mod q).
p and q are distinct primes that both divide M<sup>de</sup> − M, so pq | M<sup>de</sup> − M, i.e. M<sup>de</sup> ≡ M (mod n).
Hence Cᵈ ≡ M (mod n), and since 0 ≤ M < n, reducing Cᵈ modulo n returns exactly M.
distractors: Since de ≡ 1 (mod n), write de = 1 + tn with an integer t ≥ 0.
Since p ∤ M, Fermat’s little theorem gives M<sup>p</sup> ≡ 1 (mod p).
Since M<sup>de</sup> ≡ M modulo p and modulo q, we get M<sup>de</sup> ≡ M (mod p + q).

parsons.title: Uniqueness in the Chinese Remainder Theorem
parsons.goal: Let m₁, …, mₙ be pairwise relatively prime and m = m₁m₂⋯mₙ. Prove that any two solutions x, y of the system x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ), i = 1, …, n, satisfy x ≡ y (mod m).
lines: Suppose x and y both solve x ≡ aᵢ (mod mᵢ) for i = 1, …, n.
Subtracting, x − y ≡ 0 (mod mᵢ), so mᵢ | x − y for every i.
Since m₁ | x − y, m₂ | x − y and gcd(m₁, m₂) = 1, we get m₁m₂ | x − y.
Repeating with m₁m₂ and m₃ (coprime, since m₃ is coprime to each factor), and so on, gives m = m₁m₂⋯mₙ | x − y.
Hence x ≡ y (mod m): the solution is unique modulo m.
distractors: Since each mᵢ divides x − y, the sum m₁ + m₂ + ⋯ + mₙ divides x − y.
Since m₁ | x − y and m₂ | x − y, always m₁m₂ | x − y, whether or not they are coprime.
Adding, x + y ≡ 2aᵢ (mod mᵢ), so x ≡ y (mod mᵢ).

parsons.title: Inverses from Fermat’s little theorem
parsons.goal: Let p be prime and p ∤ a. Prove that a<sup>p−2</sup> is an inverse of a modulo p, and use it to find 3⁻¹ mod 11.
lines: By Fermat’s little theorem, since p ∤ a, a<sup>p−1</sup> ≡ 1 (mod p).
Because p ≥ 2, we can write a<sup>p−1</sup> = a · a<sup>p−2</sup>.
So a · a<sup>p−2</sup> ≡ 1 (mod p), which says a<sup>p−2</sup> is an inverse of a modulo p.
distractors: By Fermat’s little theorem, aᵖ ≡ 1 (mod p).
So a<sup>p−1</sup> itself is the inverse of a modulo p.
